vignette:
Linh Tran is a 22-year-old Vietnamese American woman who works as a call center agent and has been married for just over a year. She presented for therapy following what she described as a gradual but unmistakable deterioration in her ability to function at work and at home. Her PCL-5 score of 61 places her firmly in the severe range, and the picture that emerged across her intake and first two sessions was one of a young woman holding herself together with enormous effort while quietly convinced that she is failing at everything.

The assault occurred approximately fourteen months ago. Linh had stayed late after a work event, and a male supervisor offered to drive her home. When she declined to come inside his apartment, he did not accept that refusal. What followed happened in the front seat of his car, in a parking structure lit by a single flickering overhead light. She remembered the smell of his cologne, the hard plastic of the door handle she gripped and could not turn, and the taste of blood where she had bitten the inside of her cheek. She did not report the assault. He was her supervisor. She was certain no one would believe her, and she was equally certain that something in her had made this happen.

In the weeks that followed, the memory did not settle into the past. It returned in fragments - a flash of the parking structure light, the taste of blood arriving without warning while she was eating dinner, a piece of the sound of his voice that did not connect to anything before or after it. These fragments felt more present and immediate to her than anything else in her life, sharper than her wedding photographs, more real than the face of her husband across the breakfast table. She could not have explained why, but she had come to believe that this was proof of something broken inside her.

Linh's work as a call center agent places her in a large open-plan office where supervisors and team leaders move through the floor throughout the day. From the moment she arrives, she identifies where the exits are, and she positions herself so that no one can approach her from behind. When a colleague moves suddenly into her peripheral vision, her whole body responds before she has any conscious thought - her chair scrapes back, her hands come up. She has been asked twice by a floor manager whether she is all right, and both times she deflected with a practiced smile, terrified of drawing attention from someone in authority. She avoids the manager's section of the floor entirely when she can, rerouting through the long way to the bathroom. A promotion she was offered three months ago - one that would have placed her on the same tier as the man who assaulted her - she quietly turned down without explanation.

At home, the strain has taken a different shape. When her husband's family visits and fills the apartment with the noise of an easy, affectionate family gathering, Linh finds herself unable to stay in the room. She steps outside under the pretense of needing air. What frightened her most about those moments was not the sadness exactly, but the sense of being excluded from something she no longer had access to - a version of normal life that felt sealed off from her. She had begun using sexual fantasy as a way of releasing tension she could not otherwise name or discharge, though this brought its own shame. She had asked her husband not to mention the assault, and he had honored this, but the silence between them on the subject had grown into something with its own weight.

She had come to believe that if she allowed herself to think directly about what happened, she would come apart entirely - that she was not the kind of person who could withstand that. She had come to believe she was inadequate in some fundamental way that the assault had revealed rather than caused. What finally brought her to seek help was an ambulance passing her bus stop one morning, its siren cutting through the street noise, and finding herself on her knees on the pavement without knowing how she had gotten there. She came to therapy not quite hoping to recover, but hoping, cautiously, to be told that trying was still possible.
